newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - UES gets young boss, loosens insider control.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UES gets young boss, loosens insider control.

text.p: Russia's biggest company, power utility UES, elected a 29-year-old reformer as chief executive on Friday and struck down rules limiting outsider intervention in steps sure to please foreign investors.
Shareholders of Unified Energy System abolished a company rule which sharply limited voting rights of large shareholders at the annual meeting.
Previously shareholders needed written permission from the company to exercise voting rights on more than one percent of voting shares.

Boris Brevnov, a young home-town ally of First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, who is also Energy Minister, became chief executive. He replaced Anatoly Dyakov, who retained the chairmanship of the board of directors.
Shareholders unexpectedly elected Dyakov honorary president, to loud applause, while Brevnov's election was greeted with only polite clapping.
Foreign investors have hailed earlier appointments in UES of Brevnov and representatives of the government, which holds a 52.7 percent stake in the company.
UES, the most widely traded share on the Russian Trading System on Friday, rose to $0.3179 at the end of the day from $0.3115 at the close on Thursday. It was about eight cents last December.
First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais pointed to reform of UES and other natural monopolies as among its leading accomplishments during three months in office.

"We are trying to be more aggressive and speed up decision-making -- now there are important results," he told a news conference in referrence to reforms. He said the government would soon consider specific reforms at UES.

Russia has promised not to break up UES, Russia's largest company by sales, which owns and operates the national electricity transmission grid, operates 27 of Russia's 34 largest power plants and controls most regional utilities.

Brevnov's arrival shows a more shareholder-friendly style at UES, which earlier this month launched an issue of Global Depositary Receipts (GDRs), share look-alikes which trade abroad and were snapped up by foreign investors.

Dyakov said UES would soon issue long anticipated level-one American Depositary Receipts, which will trade in more markets than GDRs. The company also plans to issue a eurobond by the end of the year.
Shareholders confirmed Price Waterhouse as auditor.
Foreigners hold 28 percent of UES, Brevnov's office said, including 11.2 percent held by CS First Boston.
Market-oriented officials are struggling with poor productivity, a tangle of debts and conflicts posed by control of both transmission and generation subsidiaries.
"To create this market sensibly, without destroying the whole system, is an extremely difficult task for the state," Nemtsov said last week.

Brevnov and government allies must plot a careful course between controlling reform from the top and fostering competition by breaking down UES's control over subsidiaries in every area of the industry.
